Across today's crises, humanitarian constraints are often not the result of a lack of technical solutions. So the practical question for our discussion today is, how can diplomacy help create, protect, and sustain the space for principled humanitarian action? We're not suggesting that diplomacy can replace humanitarian action or political processes. Rather, we want to explore how member states, regional actors, and humanitarian organizations can better connect political engagement with concrete outcomes for civilians, such as safer access, stronger protection, continuity of essential services, and a more predictable environment for humanitarian operations. Our distinguished speakers bring practical experience from a range of contexts, from arrangements that helped widen humanitarian access following the Syria earthquakes to the broader humanitarian implications of the Black Sea Grain Initiative to sustain diplomatic engagement in complex crises across the Middle East and beyond. CARES relieves important humanitarian work, and Saudi Arabia's wider contribution to dialogue, peace, and humanitarian response demonstrate how diplomacy and humanitarian action can reinforce each other. The premise of today's discussion is compelling. In many contemporary issues, humanitarian constraints are increasingly political rather than merely operational. Diplomacy must therefore help create the space in which humanitarian action becomes possible. For Pakistan, this begins with prevention. The best humanitarian response is one that prevents humanitarian suffering before it occurs. This conviction underpinned Pakistan's initiative that led to the unanimous adoption of Security Council Resolution 2788 last year on strengthening mechanisms for peaceful settlement of disputes. The resolution reaffirmed the importance of preventive diplomacy and more effective use of the peaceful settlement mechanisms available under the UN Charter. Pakistan's conduct demonstrates what we have always advocated, preventive diplomacy, mediation, and peaceful settlement of disputes. Most recently, amid the escalating tensions between Iran and the United States, Pakistan, together with its regional partners, used its relationships with both sides to facilitate engagement and de-escalation. Our objective was to prevent further escalation, save lives, avert an even greater humanitarian catastrophe, and create space for a peaceful way forward. The preventive humanitarian diplomacy is evident across the conflicts and productive disputes confronting us today, from Sudan, Syria, and Yemen, to Ukraine, Palestine, and Jammu and Kashmir. These situations differ in their origins and circumstances, but each reminds us of the human cost when diplomacy fails. Conflicts persist and political solutions remain elusive. In Gaza, in particular, the immense suffering of civilians underscores the urgency of translating diplomatic engagement into sustained humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and a credible path towards a just and lasting peace. I would like to highlight four priorities. One, we must move from reactive to preventive humanitarian diplomacy. Mediation, dialogue, and confidence-building measures should be activated early, before conflicts escalate and humanitarian needs become overwhelming. Two, regional countries must serve as the first line of diplomatic enablers. Their proximity, relationships, and understanding of local dynamics should be leveraged to build bridges and facilitate de-escalation. Regional initiatives should reinforce, not replace, multilateral action. Three, the United Nations must remain at the center of these efforts. The Secretary-General's good offices, UN mediation capacities, and humanitarian agencies should work systematically with regional actors to convert diplomatic openings into civilian protection, humanitarian access, and continuity of essential services. And finally, temporary openings must become durable humanitarian engagements. But what we cannot do is we cannot protect civilians. Again, this is where states need to come in. We need civilians to be protected from airstrikes. We need weapons to stop reaching the parties that repeatedly violate international humanitarian law or impose consequences for attacks on hospitals and aid workers. And those responsibilities lie with other actors than with humanitarian organizations and the parties to the parties in the conflict and states, but also to those who might just be turning away from them. and not reacting if others are not upholding international humanitarian law. So there is a contradiction when states that arm, finance, and shield those responsible for serious violations then also present calls for protection, tactical facilitation of aid as humanitarian diplomacies. States have leverage. You have to use it. You can collectively and individually, and you must, where violence persists, ensure that there is accountability. Otherwise, appeals for compliance just become background noise. Third, on funding, and I'm guessing that most of you know that MSF does not accept governmental funding, albeit in very rare exceptions, so this is not something I'm saying on our behalf, but diplomatic engagement might remove some obstructions, but it cannot purchase medicines, it cannot pay medical staff or rebuild destroyed clinics, and states cannot cut their contributions on the one hand and then expect diplomacy to make the difference. Funding is needed. A lot of people are in need of humanitarian aid. Therefore, just to summarize again, effective diplomacy in the service of humanitarian action must go beyond operational troubleshoot It must defend the laws, the norms, and the very conditions on which humanitarian work depends. And this enables us to actually do our work on the ground. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Secretary General. So thank you to our distinguished panel for your input. I'm going to just mention a few of the takeaways I think I got from that conversation. That the world's most vulnerable are counting on you. Use your leverage. You're stronger together when diplomats and humanitarians work together to lift constraints, to break down silos, to build coalitions, and there must be more respect for IHL, that's for sure. We're going to move to the interactive portion of our conversation now. We have about a half an hour left. There are many delegations that have asked for the floor. His Excellency, His Distinguished Representative, I first wish to express my appreciation to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for convening this important discussion. Across every region of the world, countless people are requiring urgent, effective, and sustainable humanitarian assistance as a result of conflict, natural disaster, and other crises. In light of these realities, the call for strengthened humanitarian diplomacy could not be more timely. While the principle of obstacles are a breakdown in dialogue, the absence of credible mediation, the human cost is immense. Humanitarian diplomacy, therefore, has a practical purpose. It is about creating and preserving the space in which humanitarian action can take place. It is about building the relationship, dialogue, confidence and practical arrangements necessary to secure access. protect civilians, uphold humanitarian principles, and translate diplomatic engagement into tangible improvement on the ground. Our experience demonstrates that humanitarian diplomacy is not an abstract concept; it is an essential enabler of practical humanitarian action. in Kenya, in Gaza, in Lebanon, in Syria. Wherever there is a need, we are there to serve whoever needs our help in the spirit of neutrality and impartiality. We are present in 130 countries of the world, and everywhere we work with this spirit. But humanitarian action depends not only on what humanitarian organizations are capable of delivering, but also on whether it is possible to reach those who are in need. Humanitarian diplomacy is therefore critical. We should aspire to a future in which disputes are addressed before they develop into humanitarian catastrophe, in which greater resources are invested in dialogue, credible mediation, de-escalation, stabilization, and conflict prevention. Let us therefore commit ourselves to diplomacy that opens doors rather than close them, to engagement that creates space for humanitarian action, and to international cooperation that ensure that assistance can reach those who need it most. Above all, let us work towards a future in which human suffering is not accepted as inevitable, and in which the protection of human life and dignity remains at the center of our collective efforts. Thank you so much. I'd like to give the floor next to the representative of Sudan.

I have to begin by expressing and extending our thanks and appreciation for the organizers for bringing us here together to share information and speak about humanitarian diplomacy. So thank you all for coming to support the Sudanese people. especially in this period. The government of Sudan actually working hard to coordinate closely with all the United Nations agencies in Sudan and beside the international NGOs also existing in Sudan. So we are committed to provide travel permit to all over Sudan, because even the people existing in areas under the control of the militia are Sudanese people, and they are in need for support and for assistance. The second thing, I think the most important, which exists in your 10 asks for other crossing border. But besides that, we have been allowing the Adre crossing border to be open. And in last July, we have provided and suggested to the United Nations for other crossing to be indefinitely open, but we have to form a joint oversight committee from Sudan, government of Chad, United Nations, and Spain to be oversight committee to just for the control of the border. And still, we are waiting for the reply from the United Nations about our suggestion. I think that shows how we are coordinating and cooperating with the international community. For the protection, as you see, the government of Sudan also, one of its obligation is to protect their civilians. And since 2024, the government of Sudan has formed the national mechanism for protection of civilians, including all the government agencies and departments, to look after how to protect civilians, not only from the fight, but also for other services, including education, the health sector, water sector, all the departments, to how to work together to provide services for the people of Sudan, because that is part of the protection of the civilians. And we have a quarter report, and we have been sharing that with the United Nations. And I think last month we have submitted that report to the United Nations and to your office also in Sudan. And we still are working on the protection of civilians. And the big sign, I think, for the international community to witness that, we can see how the Sudanese people flee the areas where the militia of RSF exists. and seek shelter and seek protection in the areas where the Sudanese military forces exist. And that is very, very clear. I think even from Darfur now, you can see people seek protection in the areas where the Sudanese military forces exist. So we are committed for the protection of the civilians. For the assistance, we really do appreciate the support that we have been receiving from the international community and from all the United Nations agencies working in Sudan. Really, they are doing a great job to help and to support the Sudanese people in this period. And we appreciate even the visits from high senior officials who's coming to see the situation in Sudan. We appreciate that. But at the same time, I think it is high time for the Sudanese people to move forward from emergency assistance to recovery and sustainable development, because now the big number of Sudanese people are coming back, returning to their homes, to their places, because most of the country now is safe. And now people, they want to resume their normal lives in Sudan, and they need support for sustainable development. Thank you for that update from Sudan. Next, we'll go to World Food Programme. We have Deputy Executive Director, Karl Skau, with us. Karl.

The people we serve have never been in need of humanitarian diplomacy more. More humanitarians are targeted or collateral. In Tawila, 950,000 people now with nothing. women and children who survived the atrocities of El-Fasher last year, who walked that journey of days with their children and now living in this ocean of grass huts, never-ending ocean of grass huts without the basic services and also in an area that is now hit by drought. And three, Respond quickly when humanitarians are harmed. Thank you very much, Karl, and thank you to WFP for all the work you guys do everywhere. I next pass it to the Ambassador of Yemen.

And despite the flexibility that was exhibited by the Yemeni government by facilitating the entrance of oil tankers through the port of Al-Hodeida, facilitating flights through Sana'a airports in a unilateral manner during the truce announced by the United Nations that was sponsored by the United Nations in 2023, which was testimony to the ability of humanitarian aid to make achievements, even if they were limited, and to alleviate and improve the livelihoods and the living conditions of those who need it. However, these gains remained limited and unsustainable because the terrorist Houthi militias continued to violate this truce and continued to escalate at different fronts. And this was accompanied by violations perpetrated against United Nations staff, The Houthi militias are currently holding 73 of staff of the United Nations, international organizations, and civil society humanitarian organizations. They continue to hold employees of diplomatic missions. And in addition to the continued Houthi escalation, and of course, we demand unequivocally the release of these UN staff being held. Rather, this diplomacy must deal with the root causes of conflict to avoid its recurrence. We support continued we thank the continued humanitarian support provided by the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as represented by the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center, the EU, as well as the UNDP. the United Nations Office on Coordinating Humanitarian Affairs, OCHA, and we thank them for their efforts to alleviate the suffering of Yemen and to enhance response to humanitarian needs. We stress that the need for continued support in addition to guarantee sustained and predictable funding that would enable the vulnerable societies to continue. to work. Thank you, sir.

Second, we need the protection of humanitarian workers by all parties active on the ground. Attacks on humanitarian workers are simply not acceptable. Thank you. We appreciate that. Next, I'd like to give the floor to UNICEF.

Thank you, Excellency, colleagues, good afternoon, and thank you for inviting us and for giving us this opportunity. In Sudan, in the State of Palestine, in Yemen, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, in Ukraine and beyond, children continue to be killed and maimed, deprived of education and denied lifesaving assistance. For the third consecutive year, the Secretary-General in his yearly report on children and conflict has reported the highest number of children affected by grave violations, and for the first time, its member states, its states will be responsible for the majority of those grave violations against children. Humanitarian diplomacy is a practical tool for changing this reality, to give hope to those children, and we welcome its growing attention. At its best, it can unlock access, protect civilians, and deliver life-saving results for children, but as also my predecessors, said is only the tip of the iceberg. We saw this in Gaza in 2024, when actually I was working there, when negotiated humanitarian poses enabled children to be vaccinated against polio, a disease we had not been present for more than 25 years in the Gaza Strip. And we saw it again with greater access to humanitarian access, commercial supply helped reverse famine since the ceasefire exactly a year ago. We also seen it in Sudan. where keeping the crossing open has sustained a life-saving of critical supplies, and where diplomatic pressure and engagement has further averted escalation and protected civilians. This experience points to several lessons, and allow me to say three things in terms of what we have learned. First of all, we need coordinated messages and outreach. Second, coalition of actors. The executive director of IOM mentioned the coalition of actors, of partnership, a common voice, and number three, we need also to have a focus on issue that can bridge the political divide, and the survival and depression of children can allow that space. At UNICEF, together with Member States and humanitarian partners, we are strengthening our humanitarian diplomacy to protect children, as well as supply, services and front-line workers that depend on it. As part of the UN80, we are strengthening our joint inter-agency effort in this regard. I will close with two asks, two asks to all of you. First of all, use your collective political influence to uphold international humanitarian law and protect children, speaking with clarity, consistency, and unity, and translating words into action. And number two, humanitarian diplomacy must be accompanied by political action. This is essential to address the drivers of conflict and provide longer-term solution, and not only short-term band-aids. Too many children are growing up under fire, cut off from the education and protection and hope. We cannot allow this to become normal. We cannot allow the Secretary General this year for the fourth consecutive time to mention it is the highest number of children affected. We must do more than help children survive in crisis. Thank you so much to UNICEF and for all the great work that you do. Our final intervention will be from Brazil as we're nearly out of time.

Thank you so much. We have about three minutes. Dr. Al-Rudayr, I'd like to ask you to give us some final closing thoughts.

Thank you. I will be shorter than three minutes. And let me start by thanking the EU and the United Nations and the respected speakers on this table and on the floor.
